newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Clinton in Manila for Asian summit talks.
newsitem.headline: Clinton in Manila for Asian summit talks.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton arrived in the Philippines on Saturday night for talks with the leaders of China, Japan and South Korea and an annual Asian trade summit.

Fresh from an extended working holiday in Australia, where he played golf, went swimming on the Great Barrier Reef and petted kangaroos and koalas for photographers, Clinton was ready to try to increase stability in the Pacific and open more markets for American high-tech exports.

Clinton's aim at the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum was to win endorsement of a U.S. bid to get the World Trade Organisation to agree to eliminate all import duties on a broad range of products in the information technology area when it meets in Singapore next month.

A declaration at the end of two days of ministerial talks fell short of an outright commitment to free trade in computers, memory chips and telecommunications equipment, but top Clinton advisers hailed the move.
The first big order of business for Clinton was a Sunday meeting with Chinese President Jiang Zemin, who was also in Manila for the APEC summit. It was to be the fourth meeting between the two men.

Clinton, who said in a speech to Australia's parliament last Tuesday that the 21st century would be shaped to a large extent by how Beijing "defines its greatness." planned to engage Jiang on such issues as arms control, regional security and human rights, U.S. officials said.

Secretary of State Warren Christopher established a new strategic basis for cooperating with China during talks in Beijing earlier this week and the Clinton-Jiang meeting was expected to confirm that progress.
The two leaders were expected to discuss scheduling an exchange of summits in each other's capitals and could announce dates for those events.

"Over the past year, I believe we've turned a corner in the relationship and dealt successfully with some very difficult issues," deputy U.S. National Security Adviser Samuel Berger told reporters in advance of the meeting.
Berger cited a narrowing of differences on such matters as Taiwan, nuclear non-proliferation and the recognition of copyrights.
"That process demonstrates that we can work together and work through our differences as great powers must," he said.

Clinton, on his first trip abroad since his re-election on November 5 and accompanied by his wife Hillary, planned rapid-fire meetings with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and South Korean President Kim Young-sam after his talks with Jiang.

U.S. officials said repairing strains caused by the misconduct of U.S. military personnel on Okinawa would be high on Clinton's agenda with Hashimoto, and that he would discuss the recent North Korean submarine incident with South Korea's Kim.

The submarine, on an apparent infiltration mission, ran aground off South Korea's coast and that incident, as well as a bloody manhunt for occupants of the vessel, has increased tensions on the divided Korean peninsula.
